'''''Clusia rosea''''', the '''autograph tree''', '''copey''', '''cupey''',<ref name="Puerto Rico Office of Historian 1949">{{cite book | author=Puerto Rico. Office of Historian | title=Tesauro de datos historicos: indice compendioso de la literatura histórica de Puerto Rico, incluyendo algunos datos inéditos, periodísticos y cartográficos | publisher=Impr. del Gobierno de Puerto Rico|issue=v. 2 | year=1949 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IVRnAAAAMAAJ&pg=PA306| language=es | access-date=4 January 2020 | page=306}}</ref> '''balsam apple''', '''pitch-apple''', and '''Scotch attorney''',<ref name="britannica">{{britannica|529406|Scotch attorney}}</ref> is an evergreen, tropical and sub-tropical [[flowering plant]] species in the family [[Clusiaceae]]. The name ''[[Clusia major]]'' is sometimes misapplied to this species.<ref>{{GRIN | name =Clusia major | id =315293 | access-date = 12 March 2018 }}</ref>

==Description==
''Clusia rosea'' is a tree native to the Caribbean, including the Bahamas, [[Hispaniola]] (such as in [[Los Haitises National Park]]), Cuba, and Puerto Rico, and to Florida, southern Mexico, Central America, and northern South America from Ecuador to Colombia, Venezuela, and the Guianas.<ref name=PIER>"Clusia rosea", Pacific Island Ecosystems at Risk (PIER) http://www.hear.org/pier/species/clusia_rosea.htm</ref><ref name=nativerange>"Clusia Native Range"
http://www.plantmaps.com/nrm/clusia-rosea-florida-clusia-native-range-map.php {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180313153254/http://www.plantmaps.com/nrm/clusia-rosea-florida-clusia-native-range-map.php |date=2018-03-13 }}</ref>

It is a [[hemiepiphyte]]; that is, it grows as an [[epiphyte]] on rocks or other trees at the start of its life and behaving like a [[strangler fig]] as it gets larger. Like a strangler fig, it successfully competes for light by outgrowing, overtopping and "strangling" its host tree with its many aerial roots.<ref name="Neal1965">{{cite book | last=Neal | first=Marie C. | title=In Gardens of Hawaii | publisher=[[Bernice P. Bishop Museum]] | date=1965 | asin=B005P0JVIW | page=924}}</ref><ref name=PIER/><ref name=nativerange/><ref>http://titanarum.uconn.edu/198500434.html uconn.edu - ''Clusia rosea''</ref> These roots are among the fastest growing known; up to {{cvt|30|cm|in|0}} in 24 hours.<ref>{{cite book |last= Moffett | first= Mark W. |date= 1993 | title= The High Frontier | location= Cambridge, Massachusetts | publisher= Harvard Univ. Press | page=90}}</ref> 

The petals are pink to white. The thin upper leaf tissue registers 'writing' giving it the common name "autograph tree". The tree produces a fleshy, light green toxic fruit; once the fruit splits, the seeds are consumed by birds and other wildlife. ''Clusia'' species are normally [[dioecious]], but in ''C. rosea'', there are [[pistillate]] (female) individuals only, and seeds are formed through [[agamospermy]].

==Cultivation==
This plant is cultivated as an [[ornamental plant]], for its flowers, foliage, and fruit. It is planted in [[garden]]s as a fruiting and [[ornamental tree]] in sub-tropical climates, and used as a [[houseplant]] in many climates.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.hear.org/starr/hiplants/reports/pdf/clusia_rosea.pdf|title=www.hear.org - ''Clusia rosea''}}</ref>

[[Image:Autograph tree (Clusia rosea)- leaf with autograph, flower, fresh fruit, and dried fruit.jpg|thumb|''Clusia rosea'' (clockwise from top left): an autographed leaf, a flower, dried fruit, and fresh fruit]]

==Invasiveness==
''Clusia rosea'' has become a great threat to Sri Lanka, Hawaii, and many other tropical countries as an invasive plant.

In Sri Lanka it is spreading rapidly on the mountains of the central hill country. It especially grows on rocks and rock outcrops where it forms dense thickets. Being a hemiepiphyte that resembles a [[strangling fig]], it also sprouts on branches and trunks of native trees and rapidly overgrows and strangles them. It therefore poses a great threat to what little remains of the native submontane forests, and the unique native vegetation around rock outcrops, such as on the Hantana mountain range near Kandy. It is known as Gal Goraka (ගල් ගොරක) or Gal Idda (ගල් ඉද්ද) in [[Sinhala language|Sinhalese]].<ref>Lalith Gunasekera, ''Invasive Plants: A guide to the identification of the most invasive plants of Sri Lanka'', Colombo 2009, p. 84–85.</ref><ref>Nimal Gunatilleke, Rohan Pethiyagoda and [[Savitri Gunatilleke]], "Biodiversity of Sri Lanka" http://thakshana.nsf.ac.lk/pdf/JNSF-36(Special)/JNSF-36(Special)-25.pdf{{Dead link|date=July 2020 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}.</ref><ref>N.D.R. Weerawardane, "Status of Forest Invasive Species in Sri Lanka", http://www.apfisn.net/sites/all/themes/framework/country_report/Srilanka.pdf {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170721191342/http://apfisn.net/sites/all/themes/framework/country_report/Srilanka.pdf |date=2017-07-21 }}</ref>

It is one of Hawaii's most invasive plants and grows in forests and open, disturbed areas in low elevations. It is spread by birds which eat its fruits.<ref name=PIER/><ref name=nativerange/><ref>"Autograph tree: Clusia rosea" at "Hawaii's Most Invasive Horticultural Plants" at http://www.state.hi.us/dlnr/dofaw/hortweeds/species/cluros.htm {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120319091729/http://www.state.hi.us/dlnr/dofaw/hortweeds/species/cluros.htm |date=2012-03-19 }}</ref>

''Clusia rosea'' is highly tolerant to extreme environments such as excessive salty winds and sprays and drought.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.fnps.org/plant/clusia-rosea | title=Florida Native Plant Society (FNPS) }}</ref>

==Uses==
The leaves were used to make [[playing card]]s in the West Indies. Some sign their autographs on the leaves and watch them grow.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hargreaves|first1=Dorothy|last2=Hargreaves|first2=Bob|title=Tropical Trees of Hawaii|year=1964|publisher=Hargreaves|location=Kailua, Hawaii|page=3}}</ref>

In Puerto Rico, in the past, parts of the plant were used to make game balls, to make tar and for firewood.<ref name="Puerto Rico Office of Historian 1949"/>
